'''Tibor Gánti''' (10 September 1933 &ndash; 15 April 2009) was a Hungarian [[theoretical biologist]] and [[biochemist]], who is best known for his theory of the [[chemoton]], a model for defining the minimal nature of life.<ref name="NG-20201214">{{cite journal |last1=Marshall |first1=Michael |title=He may have found the key to the origins of life. So why have so few heard of him? |journal=National Geographic |date=14 December 2020 |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/2020/12/he-may-have-found-the-key-to-origins-of-life-tibor-ganti-chemoton/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201214121714/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/2020/12/he-may-have-found-the-key-to-origins-of-life-tibor-ganti-chemoton/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 14, 2020 |access-date=15 December 2020}}</ref> He taught industrial biochemistry at [[ELTE Faculty of Science|Faculty of Science]] of the [[Eötvös Loránd University|Eötvös University]], and theoretical biology at [[Gödöllő|University of Gödöllő]], [[József Attila University]], and Eötvös University.<ref>{{cite web| author= Szathmáry Eörs |title=GÁNTI TIBOR 1933–2009 |date= 9 July 2009| url= http://www.matud.iif.hu/2009/09jul/18.htm |work=Magyar Tudomány |publisher=A Magyar Tudományos Akadémia |access-date= 29 August 2013}}</ref><ref name=chemo>{{cite web|author=Chemoton|title=CURRICULUM VITAE: Tibor Gánti|url=http://www.chemoton.com/eng6.html|work=chemoton.com|access-date=29 August 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110912073942/http://www.chemoton.com/eng6.html|archive-date=12 September 2011}}</ref>


[[File:Gánti Tibor Vác Köztársaság5.jpg|thumb|Plaque honoring Gánti at his birth site]]

==Biography==

Tibor Gánti worked as laboratory assistant at the Bacteriological Laboratory, Factory of Canned Food at [[Dunakeszi]] from 1951-1952. He then moved to Photochemical Research Institute of [[Vác]] in 1953-1954. From 1958 to 1965 he was the head of Yeast Laboratory, Yeast Factory, [[Budapest]]. In the meantime he completed a diploma in chemical engineering from the Technical University of Budapest in 1958, and a [[doctor of technology|Dr. techn.]] (PhD) in 1962. Between 1965 and 1974 he was the head of biochemical department at the Reanal Factory of Laboratory Chemicals in Budapest. He was awarded a doctorate in biological science by the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]] in 1980.<ref name=chemo/> 

===Academic career===

Gánti joined [[Eötvös Loránd University]] as a guest lecturer of industrial biochemistry in 1968 and taught there until 1972. In 1974, he became a guest lecturer in theoretical biology at the University of [[Gödöllő]]. Between 1975 and 1979 he taught theoretical biology at József Attila University, [[Szeged]]. He became guest professor of theoretical biology at Eötvös University in 1978 up to 1999.<ref name=chemo/>

===Chemoton===
Gánti formulated a theory about the fundamental nature of living organisms, presented as a model called the [[chemoton]] in 1971. According to the chemoton model, of necessity, living organisms should have a basic [[autocatalytic]] subsystem consisting of [[metabolism]] and a [[Self-replication|replication process]], and a [[Cell membrane|membrane]] enclosing these functions.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Van Segbroeck S, [[Ann Nowé|Nowé A]], Lenaerts T |title= Stochastic simulation of the chemoton |journal= Artificial Life |volume=15 |issue= 2 | pages= 213–226 |year= 2009 |pmid= 19199383|doi= 10.1162/artl.2009.15.2.15203|citeseerx= 10.1.1.398.8949 }}</ref>

His theory may be the most significant contribution to theoretical biology for understanding the chemical basis and [[origin of life]],<ref name="NG-20201214" /> as it provides a philosophy of [[Unit of selection|evolutionary units]].<ref>{{cite journal |author= Hoenigsberg HF |title=From geochemistry and biochemistry to prebiotic evolution...we necessarily enter into Gánti's fluid automata  |journal= Genet Mol Res |volume= 6|issue= 2 | pages= 358–373 |year= 2007 |pmid= 17624859}}</ref>

==Political career==
Gánti founded the [[Alliance for the Protection of Nature and Society]] (TTVSZ) that received 0.03 percent of the votes and won no seats in the [[Hungarian parliamentary election, 1990|1990 parliamentary election]]. He ran as a candidate on the national list of the [[National Democratic Alliance (Hungary)|National Democratic Alliance]] in the [[Hungarian parliamentary election, 1994|1994 parliamentary election]], but did not obtain a mandate.<ref name=NS>[[Dieter Nohlen|Nohlen, D]] & Stöver, P (2010) ''Elections in Europe: A data handbook'', p. 899. {{ISBN|978-3-8329-5609-7}}</ref>

==Awards==
*1982 Herman Otto prize
*1986 MTESz prize
*1989 Pro Natura medal

* ''Chemotonelmélet II. Az élő rendszerek elmélete'' (1989), OMIKK, Budapest
* ''The Principles of Life'' (2003), Oxford University Press, {{ISBN|9780198507260}}
* ''Chemoton Theory. Vol. I. Theory of Fluid Machineries'' (2003), Kluwer Academic/Plenum Publishers, New York
* ''Chemoton Theory. Vol. II. Theory of Living Systems'' (2003), Kluwer Academic/Plenum Publishers, New York, {{ISBN|9780306477850}}
